systems.title: ticket intake with computer vision
systems.subtitle: a bot that works a fiber trouble-ticket portal around the clock
systems.summary: A fiber repair team used to open every trouble ticket by hand, download its files and check its photos. A bot now does that day and night, and the team works from a live dashboard.
systems.problem: Every ticket had to be opened, its files downloaded and its photos checked by a person, before any real repair work could start.
constraints: live tickets: a mistake costs someone real work
every model runs on our own hardware, with no paid cloud AI
systems.approach: Scheduled services check for tickets about 80 times a day and download each ticket's files. A small vision model I trained sorts the photos. Everything is stored in one database, and the team sees it live in a dashboard and a browser extension.
outcomes: 7,364 tickets handled between April and November 2026
2,187 photos sorted by a vision model I trained
systems.disclosure: Counted from April to November 2026. I am the main developer, from the first prototype to the system running today.

challenges.title: a language model was the wrong tool for photos
challenges.problem: First I had a vision model describe each photo and matched keywords in the description. It was brittle: "a small opening" was read as "open box". Then two large models in a row, one to describe and one to classify. More accurate, but slow and heavy.
challenges.solution: I trained a small YOLO11 classifier instead. It is fast, gives the same answer every time and is cheap to run. This is what runs today.

challenges.title: several services working at once
challenges.problem: Each kind of ticket has its own scheduled service, and left alone they got in each other's way.
challenges.solution: A shared lock, staggered start times, and one clear owner for each step.

challenges.title: outgrowing the first version
challenges.problem: The prototype kept its state in a single file, which was fragile once the bot ran all day.
challenges.solution: I moved it to a proper database in phases, behind feature flags, without stopping the bot.

systems.title: on-premise RAG assistant
systems.subtitle: answers staff questions about policies, people and internal tools, on our own server
systems.summary: Staff needed answers about company policies, the org structure, the glossary and hundreds of internal tools. That knowledge was spread across documents and databases. I built the assistant that answers from all of it, as the sole developer, with local models so no company data leaves the building.
systems.problem: The knowledge was spread across documents and databases, and most questions were about internal tools. Many of those are counting questions, which document search handles badly.
constraints: no company data leaves our own server
runs on one graphics card, with no paid cloud AI
no answer is better than a made-up answer
systems.approach: A small model first works out what kind of question it is. Counting questions go to a database agent that can only read. Everything else goes to three searches that run side by side, by meaning, by keyword and by relationship. Their results are merged and re-ranked, and the answer is checked against the source text before anyone sees it.
outcomes: 73% of rated answers got a thumbs-up (196 up, 73 down)
the right document is in the top 10 results 97.6% of the time
cached answers about 100 times faster after I audited the system

challenges.title: some questions are counting questions
challenges.problem: "How many tools does this team use?" has an exact answer in a table. Document search handles counting and listing badly, and tools are 61% of all questions.
challenges.solution: A LangGraph agent answers them with SQL. It can only read, only from an approved list of tables. If it fails, normal search answers instead.

challenges.title: a model will answer even when it has nothing
challenges.problem: Without a check, the model fills gaps with a plausible guess.
challenges.solution: If nothing relevant is found, it says so. An answer the sources do not support gets one strict retry, then a fixed fallback answer.

challenges.title: knowing whether a change helped
challenges.problem: Without a baseline, every tuning change is a guess.
challenges.solution: I built a test suite from real questions and captured the baseline before changing anything. I also audited the whole system and labelled each finding as measured or estimated.

others.title: construction-photo AI
others.body: YOLO models I trained check site photos for required evidence, and they are the ones deployed in the app. Low-confidence detections go to a person.

others.title: agent orchestration
others.body: Two tools for working safely with AI coding agents. A worker and reviewer loop with test gates fixed a 39-finding UI audit in one round for $1.96.

others.title: automated retraining
others.body: Watches the annotation store and validates labels. Training is deterministic code; the LLM only writes the report.

others.title: resource allocation agent
others.body: Chat over engineers' skills, certifications and assignments. All numbers come from a deterministic scoring engine.

others.title: GIS copilot
others.body: A "talk to your map" QGIS plugin for network design. Graph algorithms run without an LLM; generated code runs with rollback.

others.title: CRM follow-up reminders
others.body: Every summary bullet must quote its source note word for word, and code checks it.

principles.title: deterministic core, LLM at the edges
principles.body: Scores, training configs, graph algorithms and SQL safety are plain, testable code. The LLM routes, explains and writes.

principles.title: use the simplest model that works
principles.body: The ticket bot went from LLM captions to a 70B pipeline to a small trained YOLO model. The allocation agent uses a scoring engine, not LLM math.

principles.title: measure before claiming
principles.body: Findings are labelled measured or estimated. Baselines are captured before changes.
